result: Experiment 1 used fMRI to identify brain regions involved in eye-based attention during dichoptic movie viewing. The study found robust activation of the right FEF, bilateral IPS, and right SPL when participants watched dichoptic movies while focusing attention on the regular movie (C3, C30, C31). These regions showed stronger responses to dichoptic versus binocular movies in experimental runs but no difference in control runs (C32). The authors conclude these regions, part of the dorsal attentional network, are responsible for eye-based attention (C33, C34, C68), with right-hemisphere dominance (C69).
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm the fMRI findings. One reviewer states the study 'combines psychophysics, fMRI, and TMS to reveal the causal role of the frontoparietal attentional network' and notes 'the conclusions of this paper are well supported by data.' Another reviewer describes the fMRI experiment as 'showing selective recruitment of the right FEF and IPS during the dichoptic condition, in line with the involvement of eye-based attention.' The editor calls the evidence 'convincing.'

result: Experiment 2 used cTBS to test the causal role of FEF and IPS in attention-induced ocular dominance shifts. Results showed a significant interaction between test phase and stimulation site (C38). Post-hoc tests revealed significant ocular dominance shifts toward the unattended eye after cTBS to vertex (C39) and IPS (C40), but not after cTBS to FEF (C41). The ocular dominance shift effect (ODSE) after vertex stimulation was significantly greater than after FEF stimulation (C42). These findings indicate FEF plays a crucial causal role in generating attention-induced ocular dominance shifts (C5, C73, C74), while IPS stimulation did not affect the shift (C77).
evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm these causal findings. One reviewer states 'they show that, when cTBS is delivered on the FEF, but not the IPS or the vertex, the shift in OD induced by dichoptic stimulation is reduced, indicating a causal involvement of the FEF.' Another notes the authors 'claimed a causal role of FEF in generating the attention-induced ocular dominance shift' and that 'the conclusions of this paper are well supported by data.' The editor describes the evidence as 'convincing.'

result: Experiment 3 was a control to verify that cTBS effects on ocular dominance shift were not due to interference with the binocular rivalry measurement itself. Results showed no significant main effects or interactions on ODI (C50, C51, C52), with Bayesian analysis providing moderate evidence for null hypotheses (C53, C54, C55). The authors conclude that suppression of fronto-parietal cortex had no impact on binocular rivalry task performance (C56), and that cTBS to FEF did not affect rivalry performance (C75), supporting the interpretation that FEF inhibition undermined its modulatory role during adaptation rather than affecting the measurement (C76).
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorse this control experiment. One reviewer states 'A third control experiment rules out the possibility that TMS interferes with the OD task (binocular rivalry), rather than with the plasticity mechanisms.' Another notes 'all of the raised research questions were well answered' and that the experimental design is 'solid and progressive.' The control experiment is treated as successfully addressing a potential confound.

result: Experiment 4 replicated the main finding from Experiment 2 without auditory stimulation during adaptation. Results showed a significant main effect of test phase (C57) and a significant interaction between test phase and stimulation site (C60). Post-hoc tests revealed significant ocular dominance shifts after cTBS to vertex (C61) but not after cTBS to FEF (C62). This replication confirmed the robustness of the FEF's causal role in attention-induced ocular dominance plasticity.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly support this replication. One reviewer states 'the results of the new experiment (Experiment 4)...provide a very important replication of the main result, showing that even if the observed effect is small, it is robust.' Another notes 'The updated Exp4 eliminates some concerns and thus makes the results even more solid.' The replication is treated as strengthening the overall conclusions despite acknowledged small effect sizes.

result: The authors conclude that the fronto-parietal attentional network is involved in controlling eye-based attention in the dichoptic-backward-movie paradigm (C7, C111), with FEF playing a crucial causal role in generating attention-induced ocular dominance shifts (C8, C104). They claim this reveals a unique role of FEF in attention-induced ocular dominance plasticity (C85) and provides direct causal evidence for eye-based attention modulating ocular dominance (C112).
evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm these main conclusions. The editor states the study 'reveal[s] a causal role of FEF in generating an attention-induced ocular dominance shift' and calls it 'important.' One reviewer notes 'the authors conclude that the FEF is one of the areas mediating the OD shift induced by eye-selective attention' and states 'the conclusions of this paper are well supported by data.' Another describes the findings as demonstrating 'the causal role of the frontoparietal attentional network in ocular dominance shifts.'

result: Blob detection performance during adaptation showed significant differences between attended and unattended eyes (C45, C48, C63, C66) but no effects of cTBS stimulation site (C46, C47, C64, C65). The authors conclude that interocular differences in detection rate were unaffected by cTBS (C49, C67), suggesting the TMS manipulation did not impair the attentional task itself during adaptation.
evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about these blob detection findings. One reviewer notes the control experiments successfully rule out that 'TMS interferes with the OD task (binocular rivalry), rather than with the plasticity mechanisms.' The lack of cTBS effects on blob detection is treated as consistent with the authors' interpretation that FEF's role is specific to the plasticity mechanism rather than general task performance.

result: Behavioral performance measures in Experiment 1 showed high accuracy on movie comprehension questions (C27) and reasonable RSVP task performance (C28), with no significant effects of experimental condition or run (C29), confirming participants maintained attention throughout the fMRI scanning.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question these behavioral validation measures. The overall experimental design is described as 'solid' by one reviewer, and another notes 'all of the raised research questions were well answered.' These attention checks are treated as supporting the validity of the fMRI findings.

result: The manuscript reviews prior literature on eye-based attention and ocular dominance, including findings that prolonged eye-based attention can bias ocular dominance (C1, C2), that attention can enhance the attended eye during rivalry (C14, C15, C71), and that prolonged attention produces a counterintuitive aftereffect favoring the unattended eye (C17, C18, C72). Previous work found correlations between frontal neural activity and ocular dominance shifts (C20, C21).
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the characterization of prior literature. One reviewer explicitly notes the study is 'Based on a "dichoptic-background-movie" paradigm that modulates ocular dominance' from prior work. The background literature is treated as appropriately establishing the context and motivation for the current causal investigation.

result: The authors propose an ocular-opponency-neuron adaptation account to explain the attention-induced ocular dominance shift. This model suggests opponency neurons receive excitatory inputs from one eye and inhibitory inputs from the other (C88, C89, C90), with the attentional system modulating these neurons (C91). The model proposes that during adaptation, attended-eye opponency neurons adapt more than unattended-eye neurons (C97), leading to reduced inhibition of the unattended eye post-adaptation (C98). The authors speculate that FEF is crucial for this attentional modulation (C102, C103, C104), and that attention enhances adaptation (C100, C101).
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this theoretical framework. One reviewer notes 'The logic behind the neural mechanisms is solid.' Another states the study is 'self-consistent' and that 'all of the raised research questions were well answered.' While this is a theoretical model with speculative elements, reviewers treat it as a reasonable interpretation of the empirical findings.

result: The authors discuss the interpretation of blob detection performance, arguing it reflects visibility/consciousness rather than attentional modulation per se (C105, C109). They note that visibility differences between eyes were large while SSVEP differences were minimal (C107, C108), and argue that FEF inhibition would not necessarily impair blob detection (C106). They cite literature suggesting attention but not awareness modulates V1 during rivalry (C110).
evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about this interpretation. One reviewer notes the discussion section addresses 'some unresolved issues' from Experiment 4, suggesting the authors' treatment of these interpretive complexities is acceptable. The distinction between attention and awareness is treated as a reasonable framework for understanding the pattern of results.
